title: Obama budget to seek funding increases for SEC, CFTC, White House says
text: President Barack Obama's fiscal 2017 budget will seek an 11 percent increase in funding for the Securities and Exchange Commission and a 32 percent increase for the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, a White House official said on Monday. In a blog post on the White House website, economic adviser Jeffrey Zients said Obama will propose giving the SEC $1.8 billion and the CFTC $330 million in the budget. “Last year the Administration fought hard to keep Congressional Republicans from using must-pass budget legislation to roll back Wall Street Reform,” he wrote, referring to fiscal 2016. “We also fought to increase funding for financial regulators and to maintain their independence. But even these gains aren’t enough.” “And while the Administration is pushing for more funding for these regulators, we’ll also continue to oppose efforts to restrict the funding independence of the other financial regulators, including the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau,” he wrote. The Republican-controlled Congress is likely to oppose these and many other proposals in Obama's budget. On top of the proposed increases over the previous fiscal year, the budget will again back user fees to fund the CFTC, similar to the way other financial regulators are funded, Zients said. “Fee funding would shift the costs of regulatory services provided by the CFTC from the taxpayer to the very firms that benefit from the CFTC’s oversight. This is a commonsense change that is long overdue,” he said. The budget would also take steps to reduce risk in the financial sector by charging large financial institutions a fee based on their liabilities.

title: EPA watchdog widens audit of administrator's travel, memo shows
text: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's watchdog is widening a review of administrator Scott Pruitt's frequent trips to his home state of Oklahoma to cover more recent travel on military and charter flights, according to a memo seen on Friday. title: NSA chief says now is 'not the best time' for Russia-U.S. cyber unit
text: National Security Agency Director Mike Rogers on Saturday pushed back against the idea of a U.S.-Russia cyber unit, a proposal that several senior U.S. lawmakers have met with incredulity and that President Donald Trump himself appeared to retreat from after first signalling interest. Rogers said such a unit was “something that you might want to build over time were we to see changes in (Russia’s) behavior.”

title: CIA contractors likely source of latest WikiLeaks release, U.S. officials say
text: Contractors likely breached security and passed documents describing the Central Intelligence Agency's use of hacking tools to the anti-secrecy group WikiLeaks, U.S. intelligence and law enforcement officials said on Wednesday. title: Taking back control? Britain's May to give high-stakes Brexit speech
text: After months of Brexit talks that have made little headway and widened divisions in her party, British Prime Minister Theresa May will try this week to get the negotiations back on track and reassert her authority. The 60-year-old leader deliberately chose an EU city for the speech so that she can speak directly to the bloc's other 27 nations, but she faces a tough task in regaining the initiative. May has said little about Brexit since her Conservative Party lost its parliamentary majority in a June election she did not need to call, beyond voicing support for a deep and special partnership with the bloc once Britain leaves in March 2019. But days before the speech, foreign minister Boris Johnson set out his own vision for Brexit, challenging her more cautious approach and exposing the fault lines in her party and government. EU negotiators are also frustrated by what they see as Britain's policy drift. At talks in August, British officials spent almost three hours picking holes in the legal basis for the bill the EU expects London to pay to leave. Sources familiar with the presentation, so detailed that it ran to 11 pages and was illustrated with 23 slides, called it a show of legal muscle. But, as Brexit minister David Davis said, the meeting was even tetchier than the one before.

title: Ted Cruz takes the convention stage in the role of Brutus
text: Senator Ted Cruz of Texas did not come here this week to unite Republicans behind their presidential nominee, Donald J. Trump. Armed with his usual arsenal of florid oratory and blunt force, he came instead to rally them, someday, around Ted Cruz. He failed, at least for now. Determined to be more than just another speaker, and looking past the November election, Mr. Cruz spent weeks with aides crafting a speech they hoped would define him beyond his failed 2016 bid for the White House and lift his image from Tea Party upstart to a modern version of his idol, Ronald Reagan. On Wednesday he offered lofty paeans to an America that included gays and atheists, and where heroism was shown not only by service members fighting terrorism on the front lines but also by the forgiving families of those killed last year at the Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church in Charleston, S.C. Mr. Cruz is clearly betting that Mr. Trump is likely to lose, perhaps embarrassingly, and that when he does, Mr. Cruz will emerge as the strongest voice for the Republican Party's core conservative principles. title: As French cool on strikes, Macron's reforms face an easier path
text: There was a time when angry French workers could down tools and pour into the streets en masse to force ministers to back down. But times have changed, making President Emmanuel Macron's task of pushing through labor reforms that much easier. Barely 26,000 people turned out for one Paris rally against the reforms on Tuesday, a fraction of the hundreds of thousands who went on strike in the heyday of French industrial action, freezing activity across swathes of the economy. French strikes are not what they once were, reflecting a cooling of national attitudes toward union militancy as well as a change of approach by Macron, who flagged his reforms well ahead of time to union leaders whose own powers have declined. As a result, the 39-year-old former investment banker has the best chance in generations to overhaul France's labor laws as part of his strategy to revive the EU's second-largest economy. “Fundamentally it is not a very strike-prone country any more,” said Bob Hancke, a labor relations expert at the London School of Economics. In the mid-1990s, the joke was that practically everyone had been a trade union member but no one ever stayed. In 2015, companies in France lost 69 days to strikes per 1,000 workers. That was barely a fifth of the level in the late 1990s and a far cry from the 1,000 days lost to strikes per 1,000 workers in the late 1980s. The decline has sped up since conservative President Nicolas Sarkozy passed a law in 2007 banning wildcat walkouts and requiring public transport unions to guarantee a minimum service during strikes.

title: Cambodia's Hun Sen calls for arrests of opposition 'rebels in the city'
text: Cambodia could make more arrests of people linked to a plot to topple the government, Prime Minister Hun Sen said on Monday, denouncing opposition figures as rebels in the city intent on staging a color revolution, despite past failures. The remark is part of the strongman's widening crackdown on opposition politicians and independent media, which critics and rights groups regard as an attempt to bolster his party's strength ahead of a general election next year. Last month, authorities arrested Kem Sokha, leader of the opposition Cambodia National Rescue Party (CNRP), and charged him with treason and espionage over an alleged plot to seize power with U.S. help. The U.S. embassy has rejected any suggestion of interference in politics. The Sept. 3 arrest drew condemnation from Western countries, and the CNRP has said about half its members of parliament have fled Cambodia for fear of a crackdown by Hun Sen. “This isn’t over yet with one arrest, I would like to send out a message,” Hun Sen, who has ruled Cambodia for more than 30 years, said at an opening ceremony for a hotel in Siem Reap province. “This set-up is a systematic activity,” he added, referring to the alleged opposition plot to overthrow his government. “The rebels in the city that do color revolution are absolutely rejected.” Hun Sen can count on support from his main ally, China, which has said it backs Cambodia's efforts to maintain its security. The government says a 2013 video in which Kem Sokha tells supporters he has help from unidentified Americans to win power is evidence that he was colluding with the United States. The opposition says the video shows an election strategy, not a coup plot.

title: Texas officer survives being run over twice; suspect shot dead
text: An Arlington, Texas, police officer is lucky to be alive after a fleeing suspect ran her over twice. The suspect was fatally shot by another officer as he tried to get away. Arlington Police Department Corporal Elise Bowden was released from John Peter Smith Hospital on Super Bowl Sunday after an incident she did not expect to survive. The police veteran and mother of eight was greeted by a cheering crowd of fellow officers, other friends and relatives as she was wheeled out of the hospital. “I’m just overwhelmed,” she told the crowd. Arlington Police Chief Will Johnson, Sergeant Brad Norman and her husband accompanied her as she left the hospital. “Another detective from Dallas who got run over himself came to tell me, ‘You’ll survive this’,” the gutsy police officer said. “I know I will. I already did. Everything I have is mendable.” On February 1, Cpl. Bowden made a routine traffic stop. A records check on the driver, Tavis Cane, showed that he had an outstanding felony warrant from Dallas County for evading arrest. He also had several misdemeanor warrants from neighboring Grand Prairie, Texas, according to a Fort Worth report. After learning about the warrants, Bowden called for assistance, and two more Arlington police officers quickly responded. The officers approached Crane and ordered him out of the car. Arlington Police Department spokesman Lt. Christopher Cook told reporters, “She was very polite. The suspect was given so many chances to get out of the vehicle that I’d say she was begging him to get out.” The second officer, Craig Roper, opened the car's passenger door and began to climb in to try to force Crane out of the car.
